stops.note: the eggplant was domesticated in South or Southeast Asia; some scholars trace the Sanskrit name further back to a Dravidian word
reached Arabic through Persian bādingān; Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq's 10th-century Baghdad cookbook includes būrāniyya, an eggplant dish named after Būrān, wife of Caliph al-Ma'mun
inherited from the Arabic of al-Andalus, then carried to Portugal's Indian trading posts such as Goa, captured in 1510

Anglo-Indian English took the Portuguese word; Bombay itself passed from Portugal to England in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry, and brinjal is still the everyday word in India and South Africa

current_meaning: an eggplant or aubergine (in South Asian and South African English)
